summary: The five target rows are NOT one uniform block. ja.wikipedia states the divergence precisely, citing the director/character-designer interview in the BD vol.1 bonus booklet 'Aka no Sho': from episode 19 onward the anime becomes an anime-original development that REPURPOSES manga episodes (原作エピソードを流用したアニメオリジナル展開となり、原作とは異なるストーリーとなる). That is exactly what the episode data shows. Eps 20 and 21 still carry a large, story-carrying share of real manga: the akamegakill fandom infoboxes assign ch 46/52/53 to ep 20 and ch 41/42/43/51/52/53 to ep 21, and ep 21's own Notes section enumerates the adaptation beat by beat ('Esdeath's meeting with Tatsumi is adapted from her meetings with him from Chapters 51 and 52', 'her battle with Mine from Chapter 53 does not occur', a dozen listed differences at Tatsumi's execution). Both are mixed. Eps 22, 23 and 24 carry no chapter field at all and could not have carried one: the last manga chapter published before the finale was ch 54 (October 27, 2014; ch 55 appeared December 20, 2014, six days AFTER episode 24 aired). Their manga counterparts — Akame vs Kurome (ch 64-65), the Emperor and Shikoutazer (ch 74), the Esdeath duel and the finale (ch 75-78) — were all written later and end differently: Kurome lives, Tatsumi lives permanently transformed and Mine survives to bear his child, where the anime kills all three. Those three rows are filler. On Takahiro: he is credited SCENARIO SUPERVISOR (シナリオ監修), a specific act beyond a blanket 原作 credit, confirmed by ja.wikipedia (sourced to Otona Anime Vol.35, 2014-09-22, p.139), en.wikipedia and the fandom staff list. That is a real adoption argument and it is set out in the flags — but no source shows him writing or declaring the anime ending, and the source line he himself continued for two more years overwrites it, while the wiki maintains per-character '/Filler Plot' subpages headed 'Filler Events that happen in the anime only and does not constitute to the canon material'. Recommendation: no adopted{author}. One striking detail: the ep 22/23/24 titles (妹を斬る, 皇帝を斬る, アカメが斬る!) are the exact kanji titles Takahiro would later give manga chapters 64/65, 74 and 78 — the same outline, two different executions.

standings.chapters: 46, 52, 53 (fandom infobox); the Budo ambush the episode climaxes on is ch 51
standings.note: The episode's frame is manga: Honest presenting Syura and his unit to the panicking officials while Budo declares he will hold the Capital (the ch 44-48 Wild Hunt stretch, infobox ch 46), Tatsumi and Lubbock walking into the palace ambush and Tatsumi being beaten and captured by Budo with Adramelech (ch 51, whose wiki summary is that exact fight), and the aftermath — Syura reported dead to Honest, Tatsumi imprisoned, Esdeath taking custody, the public execution announced (ch 52 and 53, both read and matching). The non-source half is Lubbock's death: in the manga Lubbock is captured alive and tortured (ch 52 opens on his guard), while the anime has him drag Syura into Shambhala's dimension, kill him and fall onto spears — the wiki's Lubbock/Filler Plot page records the whole sequence as anime-only. Manga and non-manga material in one episode = mixed. Caveat on the exact chapter list: ch 44-47 have empty stub summaries on the wiki, so ch 46's contribution could not be verified beat-for-beat; the ch 51/52/53 content was verified directly.

The most clearly adapted of the five. Its Japanese title 絶望を斬る is manga ch 42/43's title, and its Notes section is an explicit adaptation diff: 'Esdeath's meeting with Tatsumi is adapted from her meetings with him from Chapters 51 and 52' (with four listed alterations), Mine's resignation and departure to rescue Tatsumi from ch 53 (changed only in where she meets the others), and eight further listed differences in the staging of the public execution — Incursio's placement, the barbed-wire hilt, how Mine enters the colosseum, how Tatsumi is freed. Chapters 51-54 were all in print before broadcast (ch 53 and 54: October 27, 2014; episode aired November 23, 2014) and ch 53-54 are the execution-rescue. The non-source material: Esdeath's battle with Najenda and Susanoo is lifted out of ch 42-43 (where it belongs to the Kyoroch mission, and where the anime had omitted it from ep 19) and replayed here, so 'her battle with Mine from Chapter 53 does not occur'; and Mine dies in Tatsumi's arms, where the manga leaves her alive. Substantial source share + substantial non-source = mixed.

The studio ending proper. None of the three carries a chapter field in its fandom infobox, unlike every episode from 1 to 21, and none could: the last chapter published before episode 24 aired (December 14, 2014) was ch 54, dated October 27, 2014 — ch 55 'Kill the Top Two' did not appear until December 20, 2014, and serialization ran on to December 22, 2016. Everything in these episodes is therefore anime-first: Kurome's coded summons and the church duel that kills her (ep 22), Run's backstory, the Emperor piloting Shikoutazer and Tatsumi's death (ep 23), Akame's Murasame trump card, the Esdeath duel and the epilogue (ep 24). The manga later reached the same three set-pieces and resolved them the other way — Kurome survives with Wave, Tatsumi survives permanently transformed and Mine wakes to bear his child, Akame leaves to find a cure — so these episodes have zero standing in the source. akamegakill's per-character '/Filler Plot' subpages (Akame, Kurome, Tatsumi, Esdeath) carry this whole run under the header 'Filler Events that happen in the anime only and does not constitute to the canon material', and ja.wikipedia calls the post-ep-19 run 原作とは異なるストーリー, citing the BD vol.1 'Aka no Sho' interview.

annotations.note: ja.wikipedia's phrase for the whole post-ep-19 run is 原作エピソードを流用した — manga episodes REPURPOSED into an anime-original development. These two rows are where that shows: the anime skips the Wild Hunt arc almost entirely (ch 44, 45, 47, 48, 49, 50 are never adapted, and ch 39 and 41 only in fragments), pulls ch 46 and 51-53 forward, and drops Esdeath's ch 42-43 battle with Najenda and Susanoo — cut from ep 19 — into the middle of ep 21's execution rescue. Adapted chapters therefore run out of order and with gaps behind them.

The branch point. From ep 19 the anime runs a story the manga does not tell, and every major outcome in this block is contradicted by the source Takahiro went on to finish two years later: Lubbock dies in ep 20 (captured alive in the manga, ch 52), Mine dies in ep 21 (survives in the manga), Budo is killed by Mine at the execution in ep 21 (survives ch 54 and dies later), Kurome dies in ep 22 (survives and starts over with Wave), Tatsumi dies in ep 23 (survives permanently transformed, and has a child with Mine). Note the outline overlap, which is evidence of a shared plan rather than of adaptation: the anime's ep 22, 23 and 24 titles (妹を斬る, 皇帝を斬る, アカメが斬る!) are exactly the kanji titles Takahiro later gave manga chapters 64/65, 74 and 78, covering the same three set-pieces with the opposite outcomes.

structure.notes: Single 24-episode component, one continuous broadcast July 7 - December 15, 2014 (Japanese air dates on the fandom pages are the Tokyo MX dates, one day earlier than en.wikipedia's). OUR rows map one-for-one onto akamegakill.fandom's 'Episode N' pages and ja.wikipedia's 各話リスト — verified by title and air date on all five targets, with no recap, special or OVA row in the way (the per-episode 'Akame ga Kill! Theater' shorts are ONA segments attached to each episode, not separate rows). Publication timeline, which is the load-bearing fact for this block: ch 51 = July 22 2014, ch 52 = September 22 2014, ch 53 and 54 = October 27 2014, ch 55 = December 20 2014, serialization ending December 22 2016 at ch 78 in 15 volumes. Episode 24 aired December 14/15 2014, i.e. the anime finished SIX DAYS before ch 55 was published — the anime overran the manga by design, not by accident. The anime also skips the Wild Hunt arc: ch 39, 44, 45, 47, 48, 49 and 50 are never adapted, and Wild Hunt survives in the anime only as Syura in ep 20. Two characters the manga carries through this stretch, Suzuka and Dorothea, are killed early / removed outright in the anime (noted on the ep 21 page), which is why the ep 20-21 adaptations cannot be read as clean chapter coverage.

flags_for_sean: ADOPTION — both readings, as required. FOR adopted{author}: Takahiro is credited シナリオ監修 / 'Scenario Supervisor' on the anime, a specific named act distinct from the 原作 credit, attested three ways (ja.wikipedia sourced to Otona Anime Vol.35, 2014-09-22, p.139; en.wikipedia 'Takahiro also supervised the scenario'; the akamegakill and agkofficial staff lists), and the ep 22/23/24 titles matching future chapters 64/65, 74 and 78 shows the anime ending came out of the author's own outline rather than a studio invention. AGAINST: supervision of a scenario is not a declaration that the result is canon (the batch-18 kinnikuman discriminator), no interview or statement was found in which Takahiro writes or endorses the anime ending as canon, and — decisively for a standing model — Takahiro's own source line ran two more years and overwrote every outcome in the block, so this material has zero standing IN the source. The community position is documented against it too: the wiki gives it dedicated '/Filler Plot' subpages headed 'does not constitute to the canon material'. RECOMMENDATION: filler for 22-24 with the divergence annotation, no adopted{author}. If you rule the other way, the basis text is ready-made: author, scenario supervisor credit, Otona Anime Vol.35 p.139.

ANCHOR RISK on 20 and 21. Typing them mixed makes them anchor-eligible, and the chapters (up to 53) are real — but a reading position of ch 53 after ep 21 would be a lie by omission: the anime never adapts ch 39, 44, 45, 47, 48, 49 or 50 (the Wild Hunt arc), so a viewer sent to ch 53 skips seven chapters they have never seen. Recommendation: accept the mixed types, but cap or withhold the end-chapter anchor on 20/21 and let the annotation carry the chapter facts. Stored ep 19 already sits at ch 36 via afg-continua, which is the conservative position and is arguably where the series' anchor line should stop.

UNRESOLVED: whether Takahiro fed the anime staff the ending he later used in the manga, or whether the anime ending was a separately designed alternative. The title identity across ep 22/23/24 and ch 64/65/74/78 is suggestive but not proof, and no interview stating it either way surfaced (the ja.wikipedia claim is sourced to the BD vol.1 booklet 'Aka no Sho' director/character-designer interview, which is print-only and could not be read directly). This is the only piece of evidence that could turn the recommendation above around; if the booklet is ever obtainable it should be checked.
